reply: Thank you for contacting TransUnion about information on your credit report that you believe comes from identity theft. We understand this is not the first time you have raised this concern, and we are sorry for the frustration that has caused. Under Section 605B of the Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. 1681c-2), we must block information that resulted from identity theft. To do this, we need four things: (1) proof of your identity; (2) a copy of an identity theft report, such as an FTC Identity Theft Report from IdentityTheft.gov or a police report; (3) identification of each account or item you believe is fraudulent; and (4) a statement that this information does not relate to any transaction you made or authorized. Your complaint did not list the specific accounts, because those details were redacted. Please send us the creditor names and account numbers for each item you are disputing, along with the documents listed above, so we can act on your request. Once we receive them, we will block qualifying items within four business days and notify the companies that furnished the information. If an item cannot be blocked, we will reinvestigate it under Section 611 of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. 1681i). That reinvestigation is generally completed within 30 days, and we will send you the results in writing. You may also place a free fraud alert or security freeze on your file to help prevent further misuse. A specialist is reviewing your file history, including your earlier submissions, to confirm whether any documents you already sent are sufficient and to make sure nothing was overlooked. We will contact you with an update.

reply:
Dear Consumer,

Thank you for contacting us about your LexisNexis consumer report. We understand you obtained your report, found what you believe is an error, and sent a written dispute by certified mail. You say a glass (GL) inquiry that was never paid appears as a Compensation (CO) claim. You also say your insurance company has confirmed it reported the item correctly. We are sorry for the frustration this has caused.

Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), 15 U.S.C. 1681i, a consumer reporting agency that receives a dispute must:
- conduct a reasonable reinvestigation, generally within 30 days;
- forward the relevant information to the company that furnished the data;
- consider all relevant information you provide; and
- correct or delete any item that is inaccurate or cannot be verified.

Section 1681e(b) also requires reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy. The furnisher, here your insurance company, has its own duty under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2(b) to investigate and report accurately.

The FCRA (15 U.S.C. 1681g) also requires us to confirm a consumer's identity before we discuss or change a file. This protects you from someone else altering your records. We do not intend this step to delay or block your dispute. We have asked a specialist to review your case. They will check whether the information you already gave, including your name, address, the last four digits of your Social Security number and your certified letter, is enough to locate and verify your file. If more is needed, the specialist will tell you exactly what is required and why, and will offer a secure way to provide it. Please do not send your full Social Security number by regular email.

To help us resolve this quickly, you are welcome to send any written confirmation from your insurance company. This could show that the glass item was an inquiry only, with no payment made, or give the correct claim type. We will include this in the reinvestigation and share it with the furnisher.

When the reinvestigation is complete, we will send you the written results. If anything changes, you will also receive a free copy of your updated report. If an item remains that you still dispute, you have the right to add a brief statement of dispute to your file. You may also file a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

We appreciate your patience. A member of our team will contact you shortly.

Sincerely,
Consumer Complaints Team

reply:
Dear Customer,

Thank you for contacting BMO (formerly Bank of the West) about the overdraft on your checking account. We are sorry that your earlier calls ended before your concern was addressed. That should not have happened.

Here is what we understand from your complaint:
- Your account held a balance of about $6.00 that you were no longer using.
- You had opted out of overdraft coverage.
- On two dates, the account was allowed to go negative and overdraft-related fees were charged.
- You did not receive notice of the negative balance.
- You learned about it when it appeared on your credit report and lowered your score.

We are taking the following steps:

1. Reviewing your overdraft opt-out and the transactions. Under Regulation E (12 CFR 1005.17), a bank may not charge an overdraft fee on ATM or one-time debit card transactions unless the customer has affirmatively opted in. We will confirm your opt-out status and the date it took effect. We will identify each transaction that overdrew the account and how it was processed. Any fee charged in a way that conflicts with your opt-out or our disclosures will be refunded. If some items were of a type the opt-out does not cover, such as checks, recurring ACH debits, or merchant fees, we will explain that clearly.

2. Checking our notices. We will confirm whether overdraft and negative-balance notices were sent, and to which address or email.

3. Reviewing the credit reporting. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. 1681s-2), we must report accurate information and investigate disputes. We will review what was reported, whether to a credit bureau, a collection agency, or a consumer reporting agency such as ChexSystems. If any reported balance is reversed or found to be inaccurate, we will request that the reporting be corrected or deleted. We will also send you written confirmation.

4. Addressing the account itself. If you would like the account closed once any balance is resolved, please let us know and we will close it.

A specialist will contact you directly with the results of this review, within the timeframe required for this complaint. Please do not pay a collection agency for these fees while our review is underway. If you have copies of any notices, credit report entries, or records of your opt-out, you may send them to us to help speed up the review.

Thank you for your patience while we look into this.

Sincerely,
Customer Complaints Team
BMO

reply:
Thank you for contacting us about the hold on your Apple Card account after your recent payments. We understand how frustrating it is to pay down your balance and then not have that credit available to use.

Here is how this works. Under the Truth in Lending Act and Regulation Z (12 CFR 1026.10), we must credit your payments to your account as of the date we receive them. That is why your balance went down right after each payment. Making the credit from those payments available to spend again is a separate step. When payments are large, frequent, or close together, we may wait until the funds clear your bank before restoring that available credit. This protects against returned payments, and it can take up to 7-14 business days. A hold of this kind does not mean your payments were missed or misapplied. It will not cause interest or late fees on the amounts you paid.

You mentioned that your payments total about $1,900 on a $1,700 credit limit. If your payments are more than what you owed, your account may now show a credit balance. Under Regulation Z (12 CFR 1026.11), you can ask us in writing to refund any credit balance over $1. We will send the refund within seven business days of receiving your request. If you do not ask, we will make a good faith effort to refund any credit balance that remains for more than six months.

We are reviewing your account to:
- confirm that all four payments ($120, $520, $600 and $710) were credited as of the dates we received them;
- check whether any credit balance exists; and
- tell you the date your available credit is expected to be restored.

We will send you the results in writing. We are also reviewing your concern that this hold is not described in your Customer Agreement, and we will point you to the provision that applies.

If you believe any payment was applied incorrectly, you may also dispute it in writing under the Fair Credit Billing Act. We are sorry for the inconvenience and appreciate your patience while the payments clear.

reply:
Dear Customer,

Thank you for contacting us. We understand you have been served with a summons over a Discover credit card account of more than $12,000 that you say you never opened, and that you believe you are a victim of identity theft. We are sorry for the stress this has caused. You should not have been told that you could only raise your fraud concern with the third party handling the account. Discover Bank remains responsible for reviewing claims that an account was opened fraudulently in its name.

What we are doing:
- We have sent your complaint to our fraud and litigation teams for review. They will look at the original application, how and where identity was verified, the mailing and email addresses on file, and the account activity.
- We will coordinate with the law firm handling the collection lawsuit on our behalf. We will ask them to note your identity theft dispute and to share with us the fraud claim you filed with them.
- We will review how the account is reported to the credit bureaus. If we confirm the account was opened fraudulently, we will close it as fraud, stop collection, ask for the lawsuit to be withdrawn, and have the bureaus delete the account from your credit file.

Your rights under federal law:
- Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA): Under Section 623, a company that reports information to the credit bureaus must investigate disputes about that information. Under Section 605B, if you give a credit bureau an identity theft report, it must generally block information that resulted from identity theft. You can create an identity theft report at IdentityTheft.gov, which is run by the Federal Trade Commission.
- Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA): This law covers third-party debt collectors such as the law firm. It lets you dispute the debt in writing and request verification of it.
- Truth in Lending Act / Regulation Z: These rules limit a consumer's liability for unauthorized use of a credit card.

What we need from you:
- A copy of the summons, including the court and index number
- A copy of any identity theft report you have filed, such as an FTC IdentityTheft.gov report or a police report
- A signed statement that you did not open or authorize the account
- Proof of your addresses during the period when the account was opened

Important: please do not ignore the summons. A court lawsuit has its own deadlines. If you do not file a response with the court in time, a default judgment could be entered against you, even while our review is ongoing. You may want to speak with an attorney or a local legal aid organization. In New York, the court's Civil Court Help Centers can also help you file an answer that raises identity theft as a defense.

A specialist will contact you directly to collect these documents and will keep you updated until the review is finished. We will send you the outcome in writing.

Sincerely,
Discover Customer Relations

How your balance and payments work: We collect on behalf of the toll authority named in our letter. You may pay the toll authority directly, as you did when you contacted them, or pay through us. Your rights: Where the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) and its implementing rule, Regulation F, apply, a debt collector must not use false, deceptive, or misleading statements (15 U.S.C. 1692e). The collector must also give you validation information about the debt. This includes the amount owed, the name of the creditor, and how to dispute (15 U.S.C. 1692g and 12 CFR 1006.34). reply:
Dear Consumer,

Thank you for contacting Experian. We understand you have sent several dispute letters this year about the four accounts listed in your complaint and that you want them removed from your credit report. We are sorry this has been frustrating, and we have opened a review of your dispute history and of the accounts you identified.

Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), you have the right to dispute any information in your credit file that you believe is inaccurate or incomplete. When we receive a dispute, Section 611 of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. 1681i) requires us to conduct a reasonable reinvestigation, usually within 30 days. As part of that process we notify the company that reported the information (the furnisher) and pass along the relevant information you provided. Under Section 623 of the FCRA, the furnisher must investigate and tell us whether the information is accurate, needs to be updated, or should be deleted. If the information is inaccurate, incomplete, or cannot be verified, we will update or delete it. When the reinvestigation is finished, we will send you the results in writing along with a free copy of your updated report if anything changed.

Please note that the FCRA allows creditors to report accurate account information to credit reporting agencies without your written authorization. It also allows us to provide your report to parties with a permissible purpose under Section 604 (15 U.S.C. 1681b). Accurate and verified information can therefore stay on your report even without your written permission. Accounts that are not yours, are reported inaccurately, or cannot be verified will be corrected or removed.

To help us complete a thorough review, please send us:
- For each account, the specific reason you believe it is inaccurate. For example, the account is not yours, the balance or payment history is wrong, or it is the result of identity theft.
- Any supporting documents you have, such as statements, payment records, letters from the creditor, or an FTC Identity Theft Report if any account resulted from fraud.
- Proof of identity and current address, if you have not already sent it.

You can submit disputes and documents online at experian.com/disputes, by phone, or by mail. If you believe any of these accounts were opened through identity theft, tell us and we will explain your additional rights under the FCRA, including blocking fraudulent information and placing a fraud alert or security freeze.

If you disagree with the outcome of our reinvestigation, you may add a brief statement of dispute to your file. You may also contact the furnisher directly to dispute the information with them.

We will send our findings to you in writing. Thank you for your patience while we review this matter.

Sincerely,
Experian Consumer Relations

reply:
Dear Customer,

Thank you for contacting American Express about your gift card. We understand how frustrating it is to have a $630.00 balance on your card and see every online purchase declined. We want to help you use the full value of your card.

Online gift card purchases are often declined for one of these reasons:

1. The card has not been registered with a name and billing ZIP code. Many online merchants check the billing address, so the card must be registered before it works online.
2. The purchase total is more than the available balance. This includes cases where shipping, taxes, or a temporary authorization hold push the total above $630.00.
3. A security or fraud review has been placed on the card.

Here is what we will do:

- We will review the card's account and its recent declined transactions to find out exactly why they were declined.
- If the card has a block or restriction that should not be there, we will remove it.
- We will confirm your balance.
- If the card cannot be made usable, we will offer you a replacement card or another way to receive your remaining funds.

To complete our review, please contact us using the number on the back of your card or reply through this channel. Please have the following ready:

- The last four digits of the card
- The approximate dates and merchants of the declined transactions

Please do not send the full card number or security code.

Under the federal gift card rules in the Electronic Fund Transfer Act (Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.20), as amended by the Credit CARD Act of 2009, your gift card funds are protected. In general, they cannot expire within five years of the date the card was issued or last loaded, and any fees must be clearly disclosed. Your $630.00 balance remains yours, and we will make sure you are able to access it.

We will follow up with you on the results of our review. We apologize for the inconvenience.

Sincerely,
American Express Customer Care

reply:
Dear Customer,

Thank you for contacting us through the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau about your Capital One Auto Finance account. We understand you object to us reporting your account to the three nationwide credit bureaus without your permission, and you have cited the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA). We have reviewed your concerns and want to explain how these laws apply.

Fair Credit Reporting Act: Section 1681a(d)(2)(A) sets out what does not count as a "consumer report." Among other things, it excludes information about transactions or experiences between you and the company providing the information. This section does not stop a lender from sharing its own payment history with credit bureaus. In fact, the FCRA expressly allows lenders to furnish information to credit bureaus. Section 1681s-2 requires that the information be accurate and complete, and it requires lenders to investigate disputes. The FCRA does not require a borrower's separate consent before a lender reports.

Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act: Sections 6801 and 6802 protect your nonpublic personal information and give you the right to opt out of certain sharing with unaffiliated third parties. Section 6802(e) lists specific exceptions to those rules. One exception covers reporting to a consumer reporting agency in line with the FCRA. Opting out under our privacy notice therefore does not stop credit bureau reporting. Our privacy notice, provided when your account was opened and each year after, explains this.

We review the information we report to make sure it reflects your account accurately. If you believe any specific item on your credit report is inaccurate or incomplete, you can dispute it in either of two ways:
- Directly with us, by contacting Capital One Auto Finance.
- With the credit bureau, under 15 U.S.C. 1681i.

Please tell us which item you believe is wrong and why, and include any supporting documents. We will investigate and correct anything we find to be inaccurate. You can also get free copies of your credit reports at www.annualcreditreport.com.

If you have questions or would like to discuss your account, please call us at the number on your monthly statement.

Sincerely,
Capital One Auto Finance Customer Relations

reply:
Dear Consumer,

Thank you for contacting TransUnion. We understand you believe a charged-off account on your credit report shows the wrong closing or charge-off date, that it contains other inaccuracies, and that you may not recognize the account. We take these concerns seriously.

What we are doing: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), 15 U.S.C. 1681i, we are reinvestigating the disputed account. We will send your dispute to the company that reported it. Under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2(b), that company must review it and confirm, correct, or delete the information. We will complete the reinvestigation within 30 days, or within 45 days if you send us more information during that period. We will mail you the results and a free copy of your updated report if anything changes. Any information that is inaccurate, incomplete, or cannot be verified will be corrected or deleted.

About the dates: Under 15 U.S.C. 1681c, how long a charged-off account can stay on your report depends on the original date of first delinquency. Generally that is seven years plus 180 days from that date. A later charge-off or update date does not restart that period. We will specifically check that the reported dates are accurate.

If you did not open this account: If you believe it results from identity theft, you can ask us to block it under 15 U.S.C. 1681c-2. To do this, send us an identity theft report (for example, one filed at IdentityTheft.gov), proof of your identity, and a statement identifying the account. You can also place a fraud alert or security freeze on your file at no cost.

About the privacy laws you mentioned: The Privacy Act of 1974 applies to federal government agencies, not to private companies. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, 15 U.S.C. 6802(e), includes exceptions that let financial institutions report account information to consumer reporting agencies under the FCRA without the consumer's consent. For that reason, consent alone is not the deciding factor. However, the FCRA does require that reported information be accurate, and that is what our reinvestigation will check. If you want proof of any agreement you signed with the original creditor, please ask that creditor directly.

Your concerns about damages and the impact on your home purchase have been referred for further review. If you have any documents supporting your dispute, such as statements, letters, or proof of dates, please send them to us so we can include them in the reinvestigation. You may also contact the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau or the Federal Trade Commission.

Sincerely,
TransUnion Consumer Relations
